case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a recipient of a state Attorney General’s investigative (administrative) subpoena has Article III standing and a ripe First Amendment claim to sue in federal court before the State seeks judicial enforcement of the subpoena, based on alleged chilling effects and compelled disclosure of donor/supporter information.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (standing/ripeness requirements) and the First Amendment (speech and associational rights as applied to compelled disclosure and chilling effects), arising in the context of New Jersey’s Attorney General investigatory subpoena power (issued under state consumer protection/enforcement authority).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: First Choice argues that the Attorney General’s investigative subpoena—especially to the extent it demands sensitive supporter/donor-identifying information—creates an immediate and objectively reasonable chilling effect on protected speech and association. Because that chill is itself a present injury, First Choice contends it need not wait until the State initiates an enforcement proceeding in state court to obtain federal judicial review. Petitioner also pushes back on characterizing the dispute as merely “premature” or “prudential,” emphasizing that Article III injury can be satisfied by chilled speech/association and that federal courts routinely allow pre-enforcement First Amendment challenges where state action deters protected activity long before formal penalties are imposed.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General argues that an administrative subpoena of this kind does not itself impose a legally enforceable obligation to produce materials; any compulsion occurs only if and when the State goes to court to enforce the subpoena. Therefore, respondent contends there is no sufficiently imminent or concrete injury at the time of issuance to satisfy Article III, and any asserted chill is too speculative absent an enforcement action. The State further maintains that the proper safeguards are procedural (e.g., resisting enforcement, showing irreparable harm if seeking interim relief) and that allowing immediate federal suits would improperly convert routine investigative steps into federal constitutional cases—especially when state courts can address objections in enforcement proceedings.
key_precedents: Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kagan are right to press Reisman and Standard Oil as channeling most challenges to non-self-executing investigative demands into later enforcement proceedings, and their workability/federalism concerns are substantial. But I read Reisman’s “visits no injury” rationale as turning on the adequacy of the later review path for the type of burden there—ordinary compliance costs—not as a categorical Article III rule that forecloses pre-enforcement review where the very demand predictably chills First Amendment association. Justice Barrett’s point that compelled disclosure of donor/member identities produces a present, irreparable associational injury (NAACP v. Alabama; Americans for Prosperity) answers the contingency objection: the harm alleged is not “future sanctions” but current deterrence triggered by the government’s demand itself. To preserve minimalism, I would recognize standing/ripeness only for subpoenas seeking associational-identifying information with plausible allegations of objectively reasonable chill, thus respecting Reisman’s general channel while carving out a narrow, precedent-rooted exception.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively analogize this subpoena to NAACP v. Alabama/AFPF and argue that an “objective chill” can occur at issuance, but that theory still depends on a demand that is legally operative here and now. As Justice Alito and Justice Kagan emphasize, Reisman v. Caplin’s point is not merely prudential channeling; it reflects an Article III limit rooted in the traditional understanding that a non-self-executing summons, where the recipient may refuse and obtain full judicial review before any sanction, “visits no injury” cognizable in federal court. NAACP/AFPF addressed compelled disclosure backed by enforceable law or court order; extending those merits cases to treat every un-enforced investigative demand for associational identifiers as a present injury would detach standing from concrete, legally compelled harm and invite federal supervision of routine investigative steps. Section 1983 may supply a cause of action, as Roberts notes, but it cannot supply the missing injury-in-fact and imminence that Article III’s text and our historical practice require.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s point seriously that a demand for donor identities can chill association immediately, and NAACP v. Alabama/AFPF confirm that compelled disclosure can be constitutionally weighty on the merits. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, Reisman v. Caplin and NAACP v. Gallion draw an Article III line where a non-self-executing subpoena “visits no injury” because the recipient can refuse and obtain full judicial review before any coercive sanction—making the alleged chill here contingent on an enforcement decision and a court order. Roberts’s proposed “objective chill” limiting principle is attractive as policy, but it is not a constitutionally grounded substitute for injury-in-fact/imminence; otherwise we invite pre-enforcement § 1983 litigation over investigative steps in tension with our nonfinal-process cases like FTC v. Standard Oil (as Justice Kavanaugh notes). Section 1983 may provide a vehicle, but it cannot supply the missing Article III injury at the moment of issuance.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Reisman v. Caplin is the strongest respondent point, but I continue to read Reisman (and Standard Oil) as a channeling principle for ordinary, non–First Amendment investigative burdens where later enforcement review fully cures the harm. Here, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, a demand for donor/member identifiers predictably chills association immediately, and the “wait to be enforced” route forces speakers—especially vulnerable ones—to endure exposure risk and deterrence that the First Amendment’s breathing space is meant to prevent and that later review cannot meaningfully unwind. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s insistence on “legally operative” compulsion undervalues the NAACP v. Alabama / Americans for Prosperity analogue: compelled disclosure of associational ties has long been treated as a present constitutional injury when the State demands it, because the deterrent effect is the injury. To address Justice Kavanaugh’s floodgates and federalism concerns, I would keep the rule narrow to subpoenas seeking associational-identifying information with plausible allegations of objectively reasonable chill, rather than opening the door to immediate challenges to routine investigative demands.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow “donor-identifying + objectively reasonable chill” test is the most serious push, and Justice Barrett is right that NAACP v. Alabama and Americans for Prosperity treat compelled disclosure as a distinctive First Amendment burden. But the opposing side’s strongest point still doesn’t answer the structural feature Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes: this subpoena is concededly non-self-executing, and—under Reisman v. Caplin and the nonfinal-process logic of FTC v. Standard Oil—issuance alone does not create a legally operative compulsion when full judicial review is available before any sanction. NAACP/AFPF involved disclosure regimes or court-backed compulsion; importing their merits intuition into Article III here would convert many investigative demands into immediate § 1983 litigation based on contingent chill rather than imminent, traceable injury. I remain unpersuaded that Roberts’s limiting principle is constitutionally grounded or workable enough to justify treating issuance itself as a justiciable injury on this record without more concrete allegations of imminent enforcement or present deterrence tied to the State’s posture.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s point that donor-identifying demands can chill association, and NAACP/AFPF confirm that compelled disclosure can be a serious First Amendment burden. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito stress under Reisman (and NAACP v. Gallion), this subpoena is non-self-executing and “visits no injury” in the Article III sense when the recipient may refuse and obtain full judicial review before any coercive sanction; the asserted chill depends on contingencies about whether the State seeks enforcement and what a court orders. Roberts’s proposed “objective chill” limiting principle is appealing as policy, but it is not anchored in the Constitution’s case-or-controversy limits and risks converting routine investigative steps into immediate federal oversight—an outcome in tension with separation of powers and federalism. Because the traditional channel for review remains available before any legally operative compulsion, I do not see a concrete, imminent injury-in-fact at filing on this record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s limiting principle is the strongest argument the other way: donor-identity demands can chill association immediately under NAACP v. Alabama and Americans for Prosperity. But those cases involved disclosure rules or court-backed compulsion, whereas here the subpoena is non-self-executing and “visits no injury” in the Article III sense so long as the recipient can refuse and obtain full judicial review before any sanction, as Reisman v. Caplin and NAACP v. Gallion reflect (and as Justices Kagan and Alito emphasize). Roberts’s proposed “objective chill” test is practical, but it still treats a nonfinal investigative step with no present legal effect as a concrete injury, inviting federal courts to supervise routine state investigations and collapsing the enforcement-action channel that has long preserved both workability and federalism. On this record, absent imminent enforcement or legally operative compulsion, the asserted chill remains too contingent to satisfy injury/imminence at filing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is textual/structural: under Reisman and Standard Oil, a non-self-executing subpoena ordinarily causes no Article III injury because the target can refuse and obtain full judicial review in a later enforcement action. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Reisman’s “visits no injury” language is best read as contingent on the adequacy of that later review for the type of burden asserted; in the compelled-disclosure setting, NAACP v. Alabama and Americans for Prosperity recognize that the constitutional harm is the State’s demand for associational identifiers itself, which can objectively chill association before any contempt path ripens. Justice Gorsuch’s history/TransUnion concern presses us to identify a traditionally cognizable analogue, and the NAACP-line compelled-exposure cases supply that analogue for treating forced identification of members/donors as a present injury, even if enforcement is a further step. I would therefore adhere to Roberts’s narrow limiting principle—standing/ripeness only where the subpoena seeks associational-identifying information and the complaint plausibly alleges an objectively reasonable chill—so we do not collapse Reisman for ordinary subpoenas while still giving the First Amendment “breathing space” doctrine meaningful effect.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kagan’s core point from Reisman—that a non-self-executing subpoena “visits no injury” because full review exists before sanctions—has force for ordinary investigatory burdens, but it assumes the only cognizable harm is coercive penalty. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, compelled disclosure of associational identifiers works a different, immediate First Amendment harm: an objectively reasonable chill that predictably occurs upon demand and is not meaningfully repaired by later enforcement review (NAACP v. Alabama; Americans for Prosperity). Justice Gorsuch’s TransUnion/United States v. Texas concreteness concern is important, but the compelled-disclosure line supplies a historically recognized, practically real injury—deterrence of association—tethered to the State’s official demand for sensitive identities. I would therefore adhere to a narrow rule (Roberts/Barrett) limiting standing/ripeness to subpoenas seeking donor/member identifiers with plausible allegations of objective chill, which preserves workability while safeguarding breathing space.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, and in the First Amendment context we have long allowed pre-enforcement review where government action plausibly chills protected speech and association before any formal penalty is imposed. Even if New Jersey’s investigative subpoena is not self-executing, it is an exercise of state coercive authority demanding production of sensitive supporter-identifying information, and that compelled-disclosure demand can itself create an objectively reasonable chilling effect sufficient for standing and constitutional ripeness at the time suit is filed. Reisman v. Caplin, 375 U.S. 440 (1964), does not compel a contrary conclusion because it turned on the availability and structure of review for federal administrative summonses (and limits on interlocutory review), not a categorical Article III bar; here, § 1983 supplies a federal cause of action to vindicate First Amendment rights without waiting for state-court enforcement. Narrowly, I would recognize standing/ripeness only where the subpoena seeks donor/supporter-identifying information and the complaint plausibly alleges an objective chill, preserving federalism by avoiding broader rulings about all administrative subpoenas.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not a subjective or speculative chill, and an administrative subpoena that is not self-executing does not itself compel production absent a judicial enforcement proceeding. Under NAACP v. Gallion, 368 U.S. 16 (1961), federal courts generally should not intervene where the asserted First Amendment injury depends on future state-court processes that have not occurred, and where state enforcement procedures provide the forum to raise constitutional objections. While this Court’s pre-enforcement cases (e.g., Babbitt and Susan B. Anthony List) recognize standing when there is a credible threat of prosecution under a law that directly proscribes conduct, that line does not extend to every investigatory demand where the State has not yet sought—and may never seek—judicial compulsion. Textually and historically, Article III’s limits bar converting routine state investigative steps into immediate federal constitutional litigation before any coercive order issues.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, imminent injury, and an investigative administrative subpoena that is not self-executing does not itself impose a legally enforceable obligation; any compulsion (and any cognizable injury) arises only if the State seeks and obtains judicial enforcement. Under Reisman v. Caplin, 375 U.S. 440 (1964), the recipient may raise constitutional objections in an enforcement proceeding without risking contempt so long as it appears and interposes good-faith challenges, which undercuts any claim that the subpoena alone creates the requisite immediacy for federal pre-enforcement review. Allegations of chilled association here are too speculative absent an enforcement attempt, because the asserted harm depends on contingencies (whether the Attorney General seeks enforcement and whether a court orders compliance). Allowing immediate federal suits over routine investigative subpoenas would convert ordinary state investigatory steps into federal constitutional litigation, contrary to Article III limits and the practical need for effective law enforcement investigations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III permits pre-enforcement First Amendment suits where government action causes an objectively reasonable chilling effect, and compelled disclosure demands for donor/supporter identities can constitute a present injury because they deter association and speech now, not only after judicial enforcement. Under NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, compelled disclosure of affiliations may operate as a restraint on association, and Americans for Prosperity Found. v. Bonta reinforces that disclosure regimes burden associational freedom even absent criminal penalties. While New Jersey characterizes the administrative subpoena as non-self-executing, the subpoena is still a concrete state act demanding sensitive information, and the practical risk of deterrence and retaliation to supporters supplies imminence and makes the controversy ripe under Article III. Lexmark’s rejection of expanding prudential barriers counsels against using ripeness/standing doctrines to force vulnerable speakers to wait for an enforcement action before obtaining federal review of serious First Amendment burdens.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, imminent injury, and New Jersey’s administrative subpoena here is non-self-executing: it imposes no legally enforceable duty (and no sanctions) unless and until the Attorney General seeks judicial enforcement, at which point the recipient can raise First Amendment objections. Under Reisman v. Caplin, the mere issuance of an administrative summons/subpoena “visits no injury” where there is “full opportunity for judicial review before any coercive sanctions may be imposed,” making a pre-enforcement federal suit unripe on this record. While chilling effects can sometimes supply injury in fact, this complaint’s asserted chill is too speculative absent enforcement or some concrete allegation of immediate, objective deterrence beyond ordinary investigative burdens, and workability counsels against converting routine investigative steps into federal constitutional litigation. Lexmark reinforces that the question is constitutional injury (not prudential ripeness), and this record does not show a sufficiently imminent Article III injury before enforcement proceedings begin.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III permits federal adjudication only of concrete, actual or imminent injuries, and a non-self-executing administrative subpoena—one that imposes no legally enforceable duty to comply unless and until the State seeks a court order—does not itself inflict the sort of traditional, judicially cognizable injury necessary for standing and ripeness under U.S. Const. art. III. History and tradition confirm that the ordinary course is to raise constitutional objections in the enforcement proceeding, and the absence of any immediate legal compulsion distinguishes this from typical pre-enforcement challenges to statutes backed by imminent penalties. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez and United States v. Texas, the lack of a close historical analogue to treating mere issuance as an actionable injury is a “telling indication” of the constitutional problem with jurisdiction here. Alleged chilling effects, without a credible threat of imminent enforcement compulsion, are too speculative at this stage to establish an Article III case or controversy, especially where state courts are presumptively competent to resolve federal defenses in any later enforcement action (Tafflin v. Levitt).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, imminent injury, and New Jersey’s investigative subpoena is not self-enforcing; any legal compulsion (and any penalty for noncompliance) arises only if the Attorney General seeks and obtains a judicial enforcement order, making the claim premature on this record. Our administrative-subpoena cases treat such demands as interlocutory and ordinarily reviewable only in an enforcement proceeding, reflecting concerns of workability and judicial restraint and avoiding converting routine investigations into federal constitutional litigation. Alleged chilling effects, without more specific facts showing an objectively reasonable and imminent threat of compelled disclosure before any enforcement step, are too speculative to establish standing/ripeness at issuance. That approach is consistent with Reisman v. Caplin and FTC v. Standard Oil’s rejection of litigation burdens as a basis for immediate federal intervention, while preserving the ability to raise First Amendment objections promptly in the state-court enforcement action.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury in fact that is actual or imminent, and in the First Amendment context a substantial, objectively reasonable chilling effect can itself be a present injury. Under NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, the “initial exertion of state power” to compel disclosure of members’ identities inflicts a constitutionally cognizable associational injury, and Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta confirms that the risk of chill is sufficient because First Amendment freedoms need “breathing space.” Although New Jersey characterizes an administrative subpoena as unenforceable until judicial enforcement, the subpoena’s demand for donor/supporter-identifying information is state action that creates immediate pressure to comply and immediate deterrence of association—rendering the claim fit for review now and not dependent on later enforcement. Lexmark’s rejection of prudential limits counsels that federal courts should not dismiss a concrete First Amendment chill as “premature” where the alleged injury is the compelled-disclosure burden itself.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III permits pre-enforcement First Amendment challenges when government action creates an objectively reasonable chilling effect on speech or association, and a subpoena demanding sensitive donor/supporter-identifying information can inflict a present injury even before judicial enforcement is sought. Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta and NAACP v. Alabama recognize that compelled disclosure risks chilling association and that this “breathing space” concern is itself constitutionally cognizable, making the claim sufficiently concrete and ripe. Treating an investigative subpoena as categorically nonjusticiable until enforcement would undervalue the practical consequences of compelled disclosure demands and would push speakers to risk exposure to obtain review, contrary to First Amendment pre-enforcement principles. While the State may argue the subpoena is not self-executing, the threatened invasion of associational privacy and resulting deterrence are sufficiently imminent and redressable under Article III when the demand is specific and directed at protected affiliations.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the recipient of a New Jersey Attorney General administrative subpoena seeking sensitive donor/associational information has Article III standing (and a ripe First Amendment claim) to sue in federal court to enjoin the subpoena before the State seeks judicial enforcement.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (standing/ripeness) and the First Amendment (associational privacy/chilling effect), as applied to New Jersey’s administrative subpoena authority (state-law enforcement mechanism for investigative subpoenas).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: First Choice argues that the subpoena itself inflicts a present First Amendment injury by objectively chilling protected speech and association (especially compelled disclosure of donor identities), so it need not wait for New Jersey to initiate a separate state-court enforcement proceeding; the threatened compelled disclosure and resulting chill are sufficiently imminent and redressable to support pre-enforcement federal jurisdiction and injunctive relief.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Attorney General Platkin argues that, under New Jersey practice for administrative subpoenas, the subpoena is not self-executing and imposes no immediate legal obligation to produce; any compulsion occurs only if and when the State seeks a court order enforcing it, meaning there is no present injury-in-fact (and thus no Article III standing/ripeness) until an enforcement action is filed; concerns about burden or disruption should be handled through merits/irreparable-harm standards (or by resisting enforcement), not by expanding Article III, and any broader right to immediate federal review would require congressional authorization beyond narrow ultra vires exceptions.
key_precedents: Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)
Platkin v. Smith & Wesson Sales Co., 474 N.J. Super. 476 (App. Div. 2023)
United States v. Morton Salt Co., 338 U.S. 632 (1950)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s Reisman-based point is the hardest: a non-self-executing subpoena with full judicial review before sanctions substantially reduces the immediacy of injury and raises the Gallion federalism/equity caution. But I do not read Reisman as a categorical Article III rule that issuance of process can never itself inflict a concrete injury; as Justice Kagan notes, it turned on that summons scheme and the absence of an immediate constitutional harm, whereas here the pleaded injury is an objectively reasonable, ongoing First Amendment associational chill from a targeted demand for donor identities coupled with a credible prospect of enforcement. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning objection underscores the need for a narrow holding, but our associational-privacy cases recognize that compelled identification can deter protected association now, independent of contempt or a later enforcement order, and standing can be confined to that context without opening the door to generalized pre-enforcement challenges to ordinary subpoenas. Gallion still matters, but primarily as a reason to craft restrained relief and avoid broad federal interference, not to deny jurisdiction where a present constitutional injury is plausibly alleged.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s “objective chill” theory, echoed by Justices Kagan and Sotomayor, is the strongest point for Petitioner, but under Article III’s original meaning a cognizable injury requires present legal coercion or a non-contingent invasion of a legally protected interest, not a deterrent effect that depends on future enforcement choices. As Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett emphasize, this subpoena is non-self-executing: the recipient may refuse with no sanction and obtain full judicial review in any enforcement action before any disclosure occurs, so any alleged harm remains contingent and not imminent. Reisman is therefore properly read as reflecting a constitutional justiciability limit in this setting, not merely a statutory-finality or prudential rule, and NAACP v. Gallion reinforces the institutional caution against federal pre-enforcement interference with state investigative processes when ordinary enforcement review is available. Section 1983 supplies a cause of action, but as Justice Alito notes it cannot manufacture injury-in-fact where the asserted harm is untethered from any present compulsion.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s “objective chill” point seriously, but it still does not supply the concrete, legally cognizable injury Article III requires when the subpoena is non-self-executing and no disclosure or sanction can occur unless and until the State chooses to sue and a court orders compliance. In that posture, the alleged harm remains contingent on future state action, and Reisman’s logic—stressed by Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett—fits better than the associational-privacy merits cases the Petitioners invoke, because the recipient can refuse and obtain “full opportunity for judicial review” before any compelled identification. Justice Sotomayor’s § 1983/Lexmark points confirm a cause of action and warn against smuggling prudential concerns into standing, but as Justice Thomas notes they cannot manufacture injury-in-fact where the only present effect is a generalized deterrence untethered to imminent compulsion. NAACP v. Gallion reinforces that we should not let federal courts short-circuit the State’s ordinary enforcement-and-review channel absent a coercive order or self-executing penalty structure that makes injury immediate.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Barrett’s Reisman framing is the toughest point, but it treats “injury” as synonymous with contempt or compelled production, which is too narrow in the First Amendment associational-privacy context. The subpoena’s targeted demand for donor identities can create an objectively reasonable, present chill—particularly for disfavored or vulnerable speakers—before any enforcement action, and our associational cases recognize that compelled-identification threats can alter conduct immediately, not merely upon sanction. NAACP v. Gallion, as Justice Kagan notes, is more about equitable restraint and federalism than a categorical Article III bar; those concerns can be addressed by narrowing the standing holding to credible-enforcement, donor-disclosure demands rather than importing them into injury-in-fact. And while Justice Thomas is right that §1983 cannot manufacture injury, it does confirm that federal courts may stop ongoing constitutional harms under color of law without forcing plaintiffs to endure the very chill the First Amendment forbids.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Barrett’s Reisman-based point remains the hardest, but I read Reisman as turning on that summons regime’s orderly enforcement channel and the absence of an immediate constitutional harm in that setting, not as a categorical Article III rule that issuance of a demand cannot itself inflict injury. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, our associational-privacy cases recognize an objectively reasonable chill from compelled donor-identification demands as a present harm—one that arises upon issuance when there is a credible prospect of enforcement, even if sanctions await a court order. Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s reliance on the non-self-executing nature of the subpoena and NAACP v. Gallion sounds primarily in equitable restraint and federalism, and Lexmark cautions against smuggling those prudential limits into injury-in-fact; we can craft a narrow standing holding limited to compelled associational disclosure demands. I therefore would not extend Reisman to negate standing where the pleaded injury is the present deterrent effect of a targeted disclosure demand in the First Amendment context.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett offer the best objection: under Reisman, a non-self-executing subpoena with full judicial review before sanctions often means no present Article III injury. But I read Reisman as a case about a particular statutory enforcement architecture and the absence of any immediate constitutional harm there—not a categorical constitutional rule that process can never inflict a present injury. Here, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the State’s targeted demand for sensitive associational information itself plausibly inflicts an objectively reasonable, ongoing First Amendment injury (a chill) upon issuance where there is a credible prospect of enforcement, even if contempt is not yet on the table. NAACP v. Gallion reinforces equitable and federalism caution (and may justify narrowing relief), but it does not negate jurisdiction where the pleaded injury is current and redressable under our associational-privacy precedents.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s contention that a compelled donor-disclosure demand can cause an “objective chill” that is itself a present First Amendment injury, and I agree that in regimes with automatic penalties or clearly imminent enforcement that could satisfy Article III. But Justice Barrett is right that this subpoena is non-self-executing: absent a state-court enforcement action, there is no legal duty to comply and no sanction—so the alleged harm depends on future discretionary steps by the State and remains too contingent under Reisman’s justiciability logic. NAACP v. Gallion reinforces my institutional concern about federal courts short-circuiting state enforcement channels when full judicial review is available before any compelled disclosure occurs; Lexmark’s caution against smuggling merits into standing does not change that the injury-in-fact inquiry still requires more than a credible “chill” untethered to present compulsion on this record. I would therefore adhere to Respondent while leaving open that different facts (self-executing penalties, imminent enforcement, or an order compelling disclosure) could produce standing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: in the associational-privacy context, a donor-identification demand can generate an “objective chill” upon issuance, and that harm may be real even before contempt. But under New Jersey’s non-self-executing subpoena regime, as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, no legal obligation to disclose or penalty attaches unless and until the State initiates an enforcement action, at which point the recipient can obtain full judicial review before any compelled production—bringing this within Reisman’s justiciability logic rather than merely a prudential finality principle. NAACP v. Gallion reinforces that we should not let federal courts short-circuit the State’s ordinary enforcement-and-review channel absent present compulsion or an automatic-penalty structure that makes injury truly imminent. Section 1983 and Lexmark (as Justice Sotomayor notes) address cause of action and merits/jurisdiction line-drawing, but they do not supply the missing injury-in-fact where the alleged harm depends on future, discretionary state choices.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett press the strongest point: under Reisman, a non-self-executing subpoena with full judicial review before sanctions often means no ripe injury because the recipient can refuse and litigate in enforcement. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor that this case alleges a different kind of present harm—an objectively reasonable First Amendment associational chill from a targeted demand for donor identities that forces an immediate, practical choice affecting conduct now, even before contempt or a disclosure order. NAACP v. Gallion, as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize, heightens federalism and equitable-restraint concerns, yet in my view those considerations go to the propriety and scope of relief (and possibly abstention-like doctrines), not to negating injury-in-fact where the complaint plausibly alleges ongoing constitutional harm under color of state law. On a progressive-pragmatist view attentive to real-world consequences and procedural fairness, I would recognize standing here while cabining the holding to sensitive associational-privacy demands rather than ordinary investigative process covered by Reisman’s logic.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury that is actual or imminent, and a subpoena demanding sensitive donor-identifying information can itself inflict an objective, present First Amendment injury by chilling association before any court-enforcement step occurs. Unlike the federal-summons context in Reisman v. Caplin, where the bar on pre-enforcement suits largely reflects limits on statutory cause of action and finality rather than a categorical Article III rule, this suit proceeds under §1983 and seeks to prevent an impending constitutional injury. NAACP v. Gallion recognizes the sensitivity of compelled donor disclosure and the availability of federal equitable relief where state action threatens associational rights, and institutional legitimacy is best served by a narrow holding: standing exists where the subpoena targets protected associational information and there is a credible prospect the State will pursue enforcement. The case can be resolved on these narrow grounds without broadening ripeness doctrine beyond Article III’s imminence requirement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury that is actual or imminent, and a non-self-executing administrative subpoena—under New Jersey practice—imposes no present legal obligation or sanctions until the State seeks judicial enforcement, so any claimed harm is contingent and unripe. In Reisman v. Caplin, 375 U.S. 440 (1964), the Court emphasized that where the recipient has a full opportunity for judicial review before any coercive sanctions may be imposed, the mere issuance of the summons visits “no injury” cognizable in court, which maps onto the absence of present compulsion here. The asserted First Amendment “chill” is too abstract without an imminent, legally compelled disclosure, particularly where the enforcement mechanism itself supplies the forum for adjudicating constitutional objections. Consistent with Article III’s limits and the Constitution’s structure of limited federal judicial power, federal courts should not entertain pre-enforcement suits to enjoin state investigative demands that have not yet been made coercive by a court order.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, imminent injury, and under New Jersey’s non-self-executing administrative subpoena practice the recipient faces no present legal compulsion or sanction until the Attorney General seeks judicial enforcement. Reisman v. Caplin, 375 U.S. 440 (1964), supports the principle that where an adequate opportunity exists to contest a subpoena in an enforcement proceeding, the mere issuance of the subpoena does not itself inflict the kind of injury that warrants pre-enforcement injunctive review; and FTC v. Standard Oil confirms that litigation expense or disruption is not itself an irreparable or Article III injury. While compelled disclosure can raise serious First Amendment concerns, any concrete injury here is contingent on a future enforcement action, at which point objections—including associational-privacy claims—can be fully adjudicated, making the federal suit premature and unripe under Article III.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III is satisfied because a subpoena demanding sensitive donor/associational data imposes an immediate, objective First Amendment chilling effect and forces the recipient to choose between surrendering protected associational privacy or undertaking costly resistance—injuries that are concrete and imminent even before a state seeks judicial enforcement. Unlike the IRS-summons context in Reisman v. Caplin, 375 U.S. 440 (1964), where Congress structured review to occur only in an enforcement proceeding, § 1983 supplies a federal cause of action to prevent ongoing constitutional injury under color of state law, and the injury here is the chill itself, not merely later sanctions. The threatened compelled disclosure of donor identities implicates core associational privacy, and delaying review until enforcement risks irreversible deterrence to participation by vulnerable speakers and supporters. Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014), reinforces that standing turns on injury-in-fact, traceability, and redressability—not on prudential limits that would require waiting for a separate enforcement suit when the constitutional harm is already occurring.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III requires an injury in fact that is actual or imminent, and a government demand for sensitive associational information can itself inflict a present, objective First Amendment injury by chilling association, even before a court compels production. Unlike the tax-summons context in Reisman v. Caplin, 375 U.S. 440 (1964), where the Court emphasized an adequate opportunity to contest enforcement without immediate compulsion, the First Amendment associational-privacy context makes the subpoena’s disclosure demand and the credible prospect of enforcement sufficient to render the claim ripe and redressable at the outset. New Jersey’s non-self-executing enforcement mechanism may bear on the merits (and on preliminary-injunction factors), but it should not categorically defeat standing where the subpoena targets donor identities and the asserted injury is present chill rather than contempt sanctions. Lexmark confirms that the standing inquiry turns on Article III’s concrete-injury requirements, not prudential barriers that would force speakers to wait for a separate enforcement suit to vindicate First Amendment rights.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III demands a concrete, imminent injury, and compelled disclosure of sensitive associational information can itself inflict a present First Amendment injury through objective chill even before a subpoena is judicially enforced. New Jersey’s choice to use a non-self-executing administrative subpoena does not eliminate the immediacy of the threatened disclosure; it merely affects the procedural vehicle for compulsion, while the First Amendment harm arises from the State’s demand backed by an asserted power to seek enforcement. Reisman v. Caplin held that federal subpoena recipients generally must press objections in an enforcement proceeding, but that rule rested on the absence of a pre-enforcement cause of action and the adequacy of later judicial review—not on a categorical Article III bar—and here § 1983 supplies a cause of action to vindicate federal rights against state officials. Given the separation-of-powers limits on expanding justiciability (Lexmark), recognizing standing here is justified because the claimed injury is the chill from compelled disclosure, not merely the prospect of future litigation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Article III, a non-self-executing administrative subpoena that imposes no immediate legal duty to produce, and carries no sanctions absent a separate enforcement action, ordinarily does not inflict a present injury-in-fact; that is the core teaching of Reisman v. Caplin, 375 U.S. 440, 447-50 (1964), which emphasized there is a “full opportunity for judicial review before any coercive sanctions may be imposed.” New Jersey’s mechanism appears similar: compulsion occurs only if the Attorney General seeks judicial enforcement, so the claimed injury is contingent and not yet ripe as a matter of constitutional standing and ripeness under U.S. Const. art. III. The First Amendment “chilling effect” theory here is too untethered from imminent compulsion where the recipient can decline to comply and litigate objections in the enforcement proceeding, and NAACP v. Gallion, 368 U.S. 16 (1961), cautions against federal injunctive intervention that bypasses the State’s ordinary enforcement/judicial-review channels. Given history, tradition, and workability concerns, the better course is to require challenges to be brought in (or after) an enforcement proceeding rather than creating routine pre-enforcement federal jurisdiction over investigative demands.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, imminent injury, and under New Jersey’s non-self-executing administrative-subpoena scheme the subpoena alone does not legally compel production or impose sanctions until the State seeks judicial enforcement. Reisman v. Caplin teaches that where the recipient has a “full opportunity for judicial review before any coercive sanctions may be imposed,” the mere issuance of a summons causes “no injury” cognizable in federal court; that logic applies here to standing/ripeness when enforcement is contingent on a later court order. NAACP v. Gallion likewise reflects the Court’s reluctance to entertain federal anticipatory challenges to state investigative demands absent present compulsion, and petitioner’s asserted chill is better assessed (and, if warranted, remedied) in the enforcement proceeding where compulsion is imminent and redress is concrete. Because petitioner can obtain judicial review before any compelled disclosure occurs, the claimed First Amendment injury is not sufficiently ripe at the subpoena-issuance stage to satisfy Article III.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III permits pre-enforcement review when government action causes an objectively reasonable present chill of First Amendment association, and a subpoena demanding sensitive donor identities can inflict that injury immediately by altering behavior even before contempt or judicial enforcement is sought. Although New Jersey characterizes the subpoena as non-self-executing, the practical consequences and procedural fairness concerns weigh against forcing speakers to choose between capitulation (disclosure) and resistance (inviting enforcement) before they can obtain federal review, particularly where compelled disclosure is itself the alleged constitutional harm. Reisman v. Caplin is best read as an equity/adequate-remedy-at-law decision tied to a “comprehensive procedure” for enforcement and review, not as a categorical Article III bar where the First Amendment injury is the chilling effect from the demand for association information. Under U.S. Const. art. III, the threatened compelled disclosure and ongoing chill are sufficiently imminent and redressable by an injunction, and NAACP v. Gallion does not require abstention where the plaintiff alleges a present First Amendment injury rather than merely anticipating a future state-court dispute.
